lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on borders, near and far
lead.head: Where the map ends, chai begins
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode outdoors, in a place that could have been anywhere. That, Varma said, was the point: “You don’t need to look at lines on maps.”
The food writer Pushpesh Pant, he recalled, carries other maps in his head, drawn for instance by which souring agent a region uses: tamarind or kokum, jackfruit or lime. {051-S01}
Yet in geography class we are handed political maps and told who we are, and that the other person is a foreigner. Varma argued that these frames, absorbed without our noticing, hold us back.
The hosts made the case that such lines are unnatural to the way people live. Then Shah offered the case against.
## Gravity, borrowed

Shah began with economics. Trade between two countries, economists found, is roughly proportional to their GDPs multiplied together and divided by the square of the distance between them: a “gravity model” echoing Newton.
Shah stretched it to all human affairs. “What people do with each other is inversely proportional to the distance squared,” he said. {051-C01}
Then he zoomed into a border, such as the one between East and West Bengal. It is not a demilitarised zone out of a John le Carré novel, he said, but a field, with a house on each side.

The two families talk, party at night, marry and do business with each other, and their children play together. Fence the field, and the person at the centre of that circle loses half their social network.
“So you’ve taken the smallest unit of that tribe and you’ve put a line through their heart,” Shah said. {051-C02}
## The abstract and the concrete

For Varma the line on the map is an abstraction. The concrete reality is people eating, drinking, marrying and being friends. “We are together on the dinner table when we have biryani and raita,” he said. {051-C03}

Europe, Shah said, shows what can be done. Germany invaded France in 1870, in 1914 and in 1940. Today people live in France, drive to jobs in Germany and carry no papers across a border with no checkpoints. He called it “the height of civilization”.

Varma invoked the philosopher W. E. H. Lecky’s expanding circle of moral concern, from family to tribe to nation to all humanity. It cannot be taken for granted, he warned, and lines on maps stand in its way.
Technology has helped. The internet, Varma said, let him move “from communities of circumstance to communities of choice”. {051-C10}
## The catch
Shah offered two cautions. Distance has died only for electrons: pots of honey and rice are heavy, and people still need to meet, share chai and touch.

And a border can break a people if the state goes all the way, with electrified fences, dogs and machine guns kept up for fifty or seventy-five years. North and South Koreans, he said, can now barely speak to each other.
Varma worried about walls built of words, rhetoric that splits neighbours living side by side. They grow sharper, he argued, where there is scarcity, no markets and an oppressive state.
His closing recommendation fitted the theme: Agota Kristof’s *The Notebook Trilogy*, set in a borderland where soldiers come and go and children try to make sense of the world.

second.label: The Texas border
second.head: Next door is Mexico
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why the nation fades as you near the border
body: Ajay Shah said the idea for this episode came alive while he read human stories from the Texas–Mexico border. One interview was with a person in a town 300 metres from a Mexican city. {#mexico}
For that person, the people across the line were friends and neighbours. Far away, the debate was about two countries and keeping migrants out. Up close, life followed the gravity law.

The nation, Shah said, is an imagined community, fictional because it is so far away. “Whereas the reality is the bloke that I meet when I wake up in the morning and who do I have chai with?” {051-S03}

quote.text: at the lived reality, you are with your people, and your people are the people near you.

third.head: How one people became two
body: Ajay Shah then argued against himself. Build the electrified fence, add dogs and electric eyes, keep it up for fifty or seventy-five years, and you can break the oneness of a people. {#oneness}

North and South Koreans today are barely able to speak to each other, he said. One is a desperately poor country, the other an advanced OECD economy, and the North does not know what to do with K-pop. {#korea}

When the Berlin Wall came down in 1989, Germans had not moved freely since 1945, and those raised in the East, it is said, still carry psychic wounds. Shah’s rule: “if you will keep the people apart for enough generations, then they will grow apart.” {051-C12}
He added: “Not that I’m recommending this to anybody who’s watching the show.” {051-J05}

p2.title: The lie of the land
p2.deck: From the gravity model to the Berlin Wall, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take apart the border, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The first law
sections.head: The pull of the neighbour
sections.caption: the gravity model of human interaction
body: Ajay Shah opened with a parable. The Lord held an accountability session and asked each profession to show it had added value. Among the economists’ claims was the gravity model. “Gravity?” said the Lord. “But that’s what the physicists do.” {051-J01}
Economists, Shah explained, found that trade between two countries is proportional to the product of their GDPs divided by the distance between them squared.

Distance must be read broadly: two English-speaking countries are effectively closer than an anglophone and a francophone one. Then the economists, “being imperialists”, generalised the law: move two people from 10 kilometres apart to 20, and their interaction falls by four times, not two. {#fourx}
## Floors apart

This is the logic of the dense city, Shah said. He claimed that even the number of floors between neighbours, the seconds of a lift ride, changes how often they meet. Amit Varma offered his own building: its secretary is a famous astrologer, apparently, and Varma does not know which floor he lives on. {051-J02}
Applied to a border, the law is cruel. By the time you are fifty or sixty kilometres away, Shah said, the line barely matters; at the border itself, half your world is cut away. {#sixtykm}
~ Shah had confessed to physics envy. Varma said he was rather an economist “who has a poet’s heart”. {051-J03}

quote.text: Borders in the real world are just that there is a field and by dumb luck some line happens here.

sections.label: India’s borders
sections.head: Honey this side, rice that
sections.caption: India’s porous borders
body: Most of India’s chattering class, Ajay Shah said, would like electrified fences and machine guns on the borders. But borders are long, and like fractals they grow longer the closer you look, so fencing and patrolling them is very hard. {#fractal}

The incentive to trade is strong. There is forest honey on one side and rice on the other, and the natural market lies across the line. Amit Varma broke in to recall a song about this from the film *Border*. “Anyway, carry on.” {051-J09}
## Wire cutters and dynamite

When a fence gets built, Shah said, someone uses a wire cutter to cut a little gap, and “suddenly you’re up and running”. Walls fare no better, Donald Trump’s included: a grappling hook gets you over, and a small charge of dynamite will blow a hole in one. {#dynamite}

Sealing efforts, he argued, contain an element of posturing by parties keen to show their base that they are policing the borders. “Realistically, it is not possible to seal off the border.” {051-C04}
~ Shah would rather amplify the half-open arrangements India already has: a free movement zone on the Burma border near Nagaland, eight border haats with Bangladesh and an easy border with Nepal.

quote.text: So walls don’t mean much, fences don’t mean much.

sections.label: The European model
sections.head: Old enemies, no checkpoints
sections.caption: Europe’s open borders
body: “To every nationalist in India,” Ajay Shah said, “I’d like to say you ain’t seen anything yet.” For the ferocity, hatred and cruelty of nationalism, Europe “gets gold medals galore”. {051-J04}

Germany invaded France in 1870 and again in 1914, and invaded and partly occupied it in 1940. {#germany} Out of the ashes of the Second World War came what Shah called one of the great civilising projects of the world, the European Union.

Today people who live in France get into a car, drive across the border without identity papers or checkpoints and hold jobs in Germany, not as immigrants but as “a first class participant” of the Union. {#papers}
The state, Shah said, should add value, as a criminal justice system does by preventing violence, but stay out of “the natural engagements of the people”. {051-C05}
## Neither French nor German
Near a border people speak each other’s languages, Shah said, as on the Gujarat–Maharashtra border. At the French–German border, the culture is neither French nor German but a hybrid of both.
~ The same logic explains a gap in the data, Shah added. The gravity model predicts trade far above the real figure in South Asia, where nation states have distorted the natural flow. {051-C08}

quote.text: So at the French German border there is actually neither French nor German culture. There is a hybrid French German culture.

sections.label: The expanding circle
sections.head: Widening the circle
sections.caption: the expanding circle
body: Amit Varma took his frame from the philosopher W. E. H. Lecky, who, he said, wrote *History of European Morals* in 1899. Its thesis was the expanding circle. {051-R08}

In small prehistoric tribes, perhaps only the immediate family was worthy of moral consideration. The circle widened to the tribe, the town, the nation, to women and to other races, and Lecky saw it as destined to include all of humanity.
Peter Singer went further, Varma said, arguing that it would expand beyond humans to include animals. {#singer}
## Not guaranteed

Varma warned against taking the circle for granted, given the polarisation and othering of recent decades. The barriers are the lines we draw: this is my country, that is another country, and soon “an evil country”. {051-C09}

He does not understand why “globalist” has become a pejorative. In sport, he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola’s teams play, from Barcelona to Manchester City, and for Levon Aronian at chess, with no tribal loyalty. {051-J13}
~ Ajay Shah called it “so upside down”. People on either side of a border are each other’s innermost circle, so the line falls through the very centre of it.

quote.text: One of the conceptual barriers to this expanding circle are the lines with which we have divided ourselves.

sections.label: Chosen communities
sections.head: A thousand fans, anywhere
sections.caption: communities of choice
body: Had he been born twenty years earlier, Amit Varma said, he would have been a much sadder person. {#twenty}

For most of history, people lived in communities of circumstance: born in a place, a caste or a class, sent to a particular school, college and office. You mostly met people like yourself, and could not grow.

The internet let Varma move to communities of choice, built on shared interests, values and passions. For creators, he said, Kevin Kelly’s thousand true fans can be scattered anywhere and still make the work viable. {051-R10} He often quotes Paul Graham’s line that it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many. {051-J12}
In media and entertainment, he said, the mainstream is crumbling, and he counts the nation state as another mainstream growing less relevant, though nationalism is asserting itself across the world.
## Atoms and hugs
Ajay Shah urged caution. There is a death of distance for electrons, he said, but “with physical goods there is no escaping the tyranny of distance”. {051-C11}
~ Pots of honey and rice are heavy. And human beings need to meet, have chai and touch: no amount of video conferencing, Shah said, can replace that.

quote.text: I could move away from communities of circumstance to communities of choice.

sections.label: Divided nations
sections.head: Walls made of words
sections.caption: walls of brick and of words
body: Korea and Germany, Amit Varma said, are what economics and political science rarely get: natural experiments. The same people were divided in two, and only one half was allowed freedom. {051-C13}

South Korea and West Germany showed the power of free markets and individual liberty; North Korea and East Germany, the tragic alternative. Varma recommended a film on the second, *The Lives of Others*, by a German director whose name he could not pronounce. “Florian, if you’re watching, I’m sorry.” {051-J06}
He sees an irony in America, too. Ronald Reagan said “Tear down this wall”; a later Republican president, Donald Trump, wants to build one. {051-J10}
## The rhetoric of division

Walls can also be built with words, Varma warned: rhetoric and ways of seeing the world can split neighbours living side by side, in India and elsewhere. Still, recalling Joan Robinson’s line that whatever you say about India the opposite is also true, he saw reason for hope.
Ajay Shah asked whether such schisms could override the immense gains from trade between two people about to do business, become friends or become lovers. {#lovers}
~ Varma’s answer was that the gains from trade need freedom to flourish. Where there are scarcities, missing markets and an oppressive state, he said, the schisms express themselves more. {#scarcity}

quote.text: words, rhetoric, language, can also build those kinds of metaphorical walls between the same people living side by side

side.boxText: Amit Varma pointed to Arati Kumar-Rao’s work on people’s lived connection with the land, a contrast to the maps of geography class. Pushpesh Pant, he recalled, carries imagined maps drawn by souring agent: tamarind or kokum, jackfruit or lime. {051-S01}

contQuote.text: And that to me is the height of civilization. Saying, yeah, you have your nation state, but don’t interfere in the lives of the people.

p3.title: Across the line
p3.deck: Four stories from the borderlands, and what each one teaches

stories.start: I should also point out that we've normalized the way things are in India

stories.caption: two Lahores
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s 2006 cricket tour, and a city of two layers
stories.head: A tale of two Lahores
body: In 2006 Amit Varma spent a few weeks travelling through Pakistan, following an Indian cricket tour and live-blogging as he went. {#lahore2006}
Lahore surprised him. At three in the morning he blogged a picture of kids playing cricket out on the street.
You could order food from anywhere. And even though it was an Islamic Republic, he said, you could get alcohol and recreational drugs “super easily”.
Apart from one or two stray incidents, he met warmth everywhere he went. “I don’t know how much of that Pakistanis would get here,” he said, “but it was wonderful.” {#warmth}

What he found were “overlapping Pakistans over there, overlapping Lahores as it were”. One layer was the Punjabiyat that Indians know well, effusive and warm, handed down for centuries and alive in the kite-flying festival. {051-S05}
The other was “a shrill harshness of the Islamic Republic State”, with its rules and laws. The two, he said, coexist uneasily.

The hardened border is itself fairly new, Varma pointed out. For years after Partition, well into the fifties, the India–Pakistan border was fairly porous: people crossed to visit relatives and came back. “It worked wonderfully well.” {#fifties}

~ He set the scene beside the European Union, where it is understood that society matters and the state is subsidiary, its job the rule of law and a few basics. In India, he said, “it’s sort of the other way around.”
stories.why: A society’s lived culture and its state ideology are separate layers. In Lahore the culture had far more in common with India than the state would admit, and the closed border that seems permanent is a recent normal.

stories.start: it first came to my mind when I did an episode with Archel Malotra
stories.end: And that made me think about the distinction between the abstract and the concrete
stories.caption: a rant that stopped mid-sentence
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Partition interview that turned on itself
stories.head: Present company excepted
body: While researching her book on Partition, Aanchal Malhotra sat with a Pakistani family in Lahore or Karachi that had suffered through it. They were sharing their memories with her, Amit Varma recalled.

Then one of them went on a little bit of a rant: Hindus are this, Hindus are that. Mid-flow, she suddenly realised that Aanchal was sitting right there with them. {051-S02} The lady turned to Aanchal and reassured her that she did not mean her.

That made Varma think about the abstract and the concrete. “The line on the map is abstract,” he said. People talking, being friends, having a drink together: “that is concrete, that human connection.” {051-C03}
~ Varma recommended her book, *Remnants of a Separation*, built from the memories of families who lived through Partition.
stories.why: Prejudice survives on abstractions such as ‘Hindus’ or ‘foreigners’, and falters when the abstraction becomes a real person across the table. For Varma the human connection is real, and the line on the map is the fiction.

stories.start: The Indian state has built some interesting concepts. They've built a bunch of border
stories.end: harmful thing for people to actually be cut off from each other
stories.caption: the border haats
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s markets at the Bangladesh border
stories.head: Cash only, barter welcome
body: India has built border haats on its border with Bangladesh: controlled marketplaces where people from both sides come together to trade. It has built eight, which Ajay Shah called pitifully small given the size of the border. {#eight}

The rule was that all transactions would be conducted only in Indian rupees. Then the traders from the other side pointed out that they had no Indian rupees. Fine, came the reply: barter would do. {051-S04}

Shah called this a healthy thing, a step forward from “some Stalinist position of saying we will cut you off completely”. On the Burma border near Nagaland there is a free movement zone with a certain amount of give, and the Nepal border is flexible and friendly. {#nepal}
~ He wants such arrangements amplified, because both countries reap the gains from trade.

quote.text: it is a very harmful thing for people to actually be cut off from each other.

stories.start: I remember during my writing course. uh one of the participants um told me
stories.end: get the rhythm of the language, get a feel of the language, internalize it
stories.caption: a student who copied Agota Kristof
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s advice to a student learning English
stories.head: Lessons in a borrowed tongue
body: A participant in Amit Varma’s writing course told him that her first language was Hindi, that she was only now learning English, and asked what she should do.

Varma pointed her to Agota Kristof, a Hungarian writer who had to flee to France during the tumultuous twentieth century and learned French as an adult. In it she wrote *The Notebook Trilogy*, which he called a masterpiece. {051-R13}

The student bought the books. Later she told Varma she had sat down with them and copied the sentences out herself, “to sort of get the rhythm of the language, get a feel of the language, internalize it.” {051-S06}
~ Some writers who come to a language late, like Nabokov, revel in it floridly. Kristof, Varma said, stripped both the language and the narrative down to their basics.
stories.why: Copying a stylist’s sentences is an old way to absorb how a language moves. Spare prose by a writer who also came to the language late makes a good model, and Varma found its power survived even in English translation.
stories.postscript: Varma first heard of Kristof when Jhumpa Lahiri, who had learned Italian as an adult, named her as a model to Tyler Cowen. {#lahiri}
